questions.q: In the Meridian Outfitters case study, what kind of failure caused the high-value case escalation problem?
options: A code-quality bug in the customer service admin's Flow logic itself
A metadata conflict -- two independently built, individually reasonable automations racing against each other on the same field because nobody coordinated them
A Salesforce platform outage unrelated to either team's work
A data-storage limit being exceeded on the Case object
questions.explain: The case study is explicit that neither Flow was badly built -- the problem was the lack of coordination between two independently developed automations touching the same field, a textbook metadata conflict.

questions.q: What governance gap let the sales team's competing Case-queue process go unnoticed before the customer service Flow deployed?
options: There was no CAB or any other cross-team review surfacing what else was already built or scheduled before this change reached production
The sales team's process was documented in detail but the customer service admin refused to read it
Salesforce blocked the customer service admin from seeing any other team's automations
The two teams were in different Salesforce orgs with no possible interaction
questions.explain: With no CAB and no shared visibility mechanism, nobody outside the customer service admin's own head reviewed the change, so the conflicting sales-team automation was never surfaced before deployment.

questions.q: Why did it take three days for Meridian to notice the escalation problem, per the case study?
options: Because Salesforce automatically suppresses error notifications for three days after any deployment
Because customer service had no customers during that period
Because the Flow was intentionally designed to fail silently for 72 hours
Because there was no mechanism to verify the declarative change behaved as intended after go-live, and no communication had been sent to support to watch for related symptoms
questions.explain: The case study attributes the delayed discovery to a missing post-deployment verification step and a missing release-communication step that would have had support watching for exactly this kind of symptom.

questions.q: Which of the following governance mechanisms from this chapter would most directly have given the change a chance to be caught before reaching production, per the case study's analysis?
options: A louder office so admins could overhear each other's work
A larger marketing budget for the e-commerce team
An environment path with at least one shared-visibility stage (such as a QA/integration sandbox) before production, instead of deploying straight from one admin's individual sandbox
Hiring more customer service representatives
questions.explain: The case study identifies the lack of any environment path beyond the individual developer sandbox -- with no integration or shared-visibility stage -- as one of the specific gaps that let the conflict reach production undetected.

questions.q: What is the main lesson this case study draws about assigning blame for the Meridian incident?
options: The failure is about missing governance machinery around the change (risk tiering, CAB, environment path, rollback plan, communication), not about the individual Flow's logic being wrong
The customer service admin should be blamed for writing bad Flow logic
The sales team should be blamed for building any automation at all on the Case object
No governance changes are needed since the Flow itself eventually worked for most records
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as a missing-governance-machinery problem, not an individual competence problem -- the Flow's own logic was fine, but nothing around it caught the cross-team conflict.
